title: 68HC11 Maze-Solving Robot

contributors.contribution: Handled most of the electronics assembly and built the custom board Jamie designed.

description: For my third-year final-term Humber project, I worked with one partner to build a 68HC11-based robot that could explore a maze, construct an internal map, and then run the maze a second time using the shortest path it had discovered. I led the software work, designed the custom controller board, implemented the microcontroller logic first in Assembly and later in MicroC, and prototyped the maze-solving algorithm in Turing before the hardware was complete.

sections.title: Two-Person Robotics Project
paragraphs: This was a two-person final-term project during my third year at Humber.
I focused primarily on the software and board design while my partner handled most of the electronics assembly.

sections.title: Custom Controller Board
paragraphs: I designed the custom control board used by the robot.
My project partner assembled and wired the board.

sections.title: 68HC11 Controller
paragraphs: The robot was controlled by a Motorola 68HC11 microcontroller.
I first wrote the controller software in Assembly and later rewrote it in MicroC after that tool became commonly used in the class.

sections.title: Turing Algorithm Prototype
paragraphs: Before the robot hardware was finished, I prototyped the maze-solving logic in Turing.
The prototype let me validate the mapping and pathfinding behavior independently of the electronics.

sections.title: Shortest-Path Solution
paragraphs: The first pass through the maze explored the available routes and constructed an internal map.
The second pass used that stored map to follow the shortest route to the goal.
My Turing prototype was the first in the class to solve the shortest-path problem before the physical robot was complete.

sections.title: Sensors and Movement
paragraphs: Optical sensors were used to detect the robot's position relative to maze walls and floor markings.
A black floor marker indicated the end of the maze.
DC motors drove the wheels and a shaft encoder measured wheel movement so the software could count travel steps.

sections.title: Maze Mapping
paragraphs: During the initial exploration run, the robot used a consistent right-turn strategy at forks while recording the maze structure.
The resulting map was stored in secondary memory for use during the optimized second run.

historicalNotes: This was a third-year, second-semester Humber College project.
The project team consisted of Jamie and one partner.
Jamie primarily wrote the software and also helped with electronics.
Jamie designed the custom control board; his partner physically assembled it.
The controller code was first implemented in Assembly and later rewritten in MicroC.
Jamie prototyped the maze-solving algorithm in Turing before the hardware was complete.
The Turing prototype was the first in the class to solve the shortest-path problem.
The robot's first run mapped the maze and the second run followed the shortest stored route.
The original legacy card describes optical wall/floor sensing, DC motor control, shaft-encoder step counting, a right-turn exploration strategy, and secondary 8K memory.
